source.version: arXiv:2606.26626v1, 25 June 2026; C&C 2026 conference-paper manuscript, full text including Appendices A-D
source.title_on_document: Reviving Reflection-in-Action: Instilling Designerly Thinking in AI-Supported Ideation through Multimodal Prompting

supplement.where: Separate supplementary material-A is cited on p. 4, Section 4; supplemental modelling reports on p. 7, Section 4.6.1; supplementary material-C on p. 10, Table 3. No supplement URL is supplied. The PDF does include Appendices A-D on pp. 17-18, which are distinct from those supplementary materials.
supplement.holds: The Latin square schedule; full modelling reports, including threshold/cut-point estimates omitted from the intent and CSI tables and the cumulative Quality model. These referenced supplementary materials were not included in the document read.

paper_design_summary: Nine design students completed an in-person, within-participant mascot-design study using Text, Sketch and SketchPlusTags interfaces to the generative-image tool SketchifAI; condition exposure was randomized and design briefs were counterbalanced (pp. 4-5, Sections 4-4.4). Participants used AI images for inspiration and drew their own products on paper, which were counted and evaluated by blinded experts for fluency, variety, originality and quality (p. 5, Section 4.5; pp. 9-10, Section 5.3).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Within-person exposure order for Text, Sketch and SketchPlusTags input modalities to the same generative-AI tool; every participant completed a task in each modality, with design briefs counterbalanced.
assignment.quote: To mitigate reduce carry-over and learning effects, condition exposure was randomised and design briefs were counterbalanced across the sample (see supplementary material-A for our Latin square design).
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 4 (Method); laboratory setting in p. 5, Section 4.4 (Procedure)

arms.name: Text
arms.description: Baseline interface: participants generated AI inspiration images through text prompts. The same nine participants completed all conditions, so arm counts overlap (p. 4, Sections 4 and 4.2; p. 5, Section 4.4).

arms.name: Sketch
arms.description: Participants generated AI inspiration images from their sketches, with no user text input. The same nine participants completed all conditions, so arm counts overlap (pp. 3-4, Sections 3 and 4; p. 5, Section 4.4).

arms.name: SketchPlusTags
arms.description: Participants generated AI inspiration images from sketches plus short descriptive text tags. The same nine participants completed all conditions, so arm counts overlap (pp. 3-4, Sections 3 and 4; p. 5, Section 4.4).

participants.who: Design students undertaking Bachelor of Design or master's degrees in UX/UI, graphic or related design fields, screened for prior AI-tool use, character/avatar design and stylus/tablet sketching experience; recruited from one institution. Each person completed every condition.
participants.quote: We recruited nine design students undertaking a Bachelor of Design or Master’s degree in UX/UI, graphic, or a related design field, via university digital noticeboards, student clubs, social media, and word-of-mouth.
participants.locator: p. 4, Sections 4 and 4.2; p. 5, Section 4.4; p. 14, Section 6.4 (analysis sample N = 9 and single institution); p. 18, Appendix D, Table D (participant roster)

ai_tool.name_model: SketchifAI; Stable Diffusion v1.5 with ControlNet-Scribble for sketch inputs
ai_tool.how_used: Participants generated visual inspiration via text, sketches, or sketches with tags. Sketch-based conditions used a fixed back-end prompt for low-to-mid-fidelity pencil-style images. Participants switched between generating AI stimuli and drawing their own scored products on paper (p. 3, Sections 3.1-3.2; p. 5, Section 4.4 and Figure 3).

task.description: Generate and sketch mascot characters for app logos and visual elements, under briefs concerning social connection for older adults, nature exploration/hiking, and music creation inspired by folk traditions. Each participant completed one brief per AI input modality (p. 4, Sections 4-4.1; p. 17, Appendix C).
task.duration: 20 minutes per ideation task; three tasks per participant (p. 5, Section 4.4).

contrasts.reported: Sketch versus Text: Table 3 reports a negative-binomial log-scale condition coefficient M = 0.20 (posterior SD = 0.33), 89% credible interval [-0.33, 0.72]. The interval includes zero. The prose in Section 5.3.1 instead prints M = 0.21, 89% credible interval [-0.33, 0.75], and reports a 74% posterior probability of a positive effect, ln(BF) = 1.03 and BF = 2.80. The table and prose values are preserved separately because they differ.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 5.3.1 (Fluency, model scale and narrative estimates); p. 10, Table 3, Fluency row, Sketch column

outcomes.name: Originality (rarity of a product's expert-coded cluster among other participants)
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: SketchPlusTags versus Text: Gaussian model condition coefficient M = -0.06 (posterior SD = 0.04), 89% credible interval [-0.12, -0.00] in Table 3. Section 5.3.3 prints the interval as [-0.12, 0.00] and reports a 94% posterior probability of lower originality, ln(BF) = -2.81 and BF = 0.06. Originality is computed for each product from the number of other participants with products in the same expert-coded cluster.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Table 3, Originality row, SketchPlusTags column; Section 5.3.3 and Equation (2); expert clustering described on p. 5, Section 4.5

outcomes.name: Quality (expert assessment of whether each product met the design brief)
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: Sketch versus Text: cumulative-probit latent-scale condition coefficient M = -0.24 (posterior SD = 0.50), 89% credible interval [-1.06, 0.52]. The interval includes zero; the paper reports no credible evidence of a reliable quality shift. Experts scored whether products met the design brief.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Table 3, Quality row, Sketch column; Section 5.3.4 (Quality of the Products)

outcomes.name: Variety (breadth of expert-coded clusters covered by one participant's products)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Equation (1) defines Variety as (number of clusters that a participant's products belong to - 1) / (number of clusters - 1). This measures breadth within one person's ideas. Products were clustered by experts blind to condition (p. 5, Section 4.5; p. 9, Section 5.3.2 and Equation (1)). Variety was modeled with a Gaussian family and varying intercepts and slopes by participant (p. 9, Section 5.3.2).

contrasts.reported: Sketch versus Text: Table 3 reports a Gaussian model condition coefficient M = -0.02 (posterior SD = 0.07), 89% credible interval [-0.13, 0.08]. Section 5.3.2 reports the same mean and interval. The interval includes zero; the paper reports inconclusive evidence of a reliable change in the breadth of products.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Table 3, Variety row, Sketch column; pp. 9-10, Section 5.3.2 (Variety); p. 9, Equation (1)

contrasts.reported: SketchPlusTags versus Text: Table 3 reports a Gaussian model condition coefficient M = 0.02 (posterior SD = 0.09), 89% credible interval [-0.12, 0.16]. The prose in Section 5.3.2 instead prints M = -0.02, 89% credible interval [-0.12, 0.15]. The table and prose values are preserved separately because they differ. Both intervals include zero; the paper reports inconclusive evidence of a reliable change in the breadth of products.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Table 3, Variety row, SketchPlusTags column, and continuation of Section 5.3.2 (Variety); p. 9, Equation (1)

eligibility.reason: Condition exposure was explicitly randomized within participants across generative-AI configurations (p. 4, Section 4), satisfying criterion 1. Only nine people were analyzed, the same people in every condition, below the required 50 (p. 4, Section 4.2; p. 14, Section 6.4; p. 18, Table D). Human-created paper sketches were counted and scored by blinded experts, satisfying criterion 3 (p. 5, Sections 4.4-4.5; pp. 9-10, Section 5.3). Excluded from core for sample size; the codebook places randomized studies below the threshold in the screening report rather than a context-evidence class.

one_line_finding: Among nine design students (p. 14, Section 6.4), Sketch showed an uncertain fluency increase versus Text (log-scale coefficient 0.20, 89% credible interval [-0.33, 0.72]), while SketchPlusTags suggested lower originality versus Text (coefficient -0.06, 89% credible interval [-0.12, -0.00]; p. 10, Table 3).
